approaches.name: Lateral parapatellar approach to the distal femur
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal lateral parapatellar retinacular and quadriceps split with medial patellar dislocation

sources.title: Lateral Parapatellar Approach To The Distal Femur
Current concepts in the treatment of distal femur fractures in adults
Surgical approaches and outcomes associated with intra-articular Hoffa fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A complete or complex intra-articular distal femur fracture requires broad visualization of the articular block with lateral plate access

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with a towel roll supporting approximately 20-30 degrees of knee flexion and the entire femur accessible for imaging.

setup.text: Prepare the full limb, ensure the incision can be lengthened enough for atraumatic patellar mobilization, and plan lateral plate insertion and proximal percutaneous fixation before draping.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the patella, patellar tendon, tibial tubercle, lateral joint line, lateral epicondyle, and femoral shaft axis.

incision.text: Use a roughly 15-18 cm anterior incision centered at or slightly lateral to midline, extending sufficiently proximal to permit quadriceps release and medial patellar dislocation.

superficial_interval.text: Expose both borders of the quadriceps tendon while preserving the extensor retinaculum over the anterior patella.

deep_interval.text: Divide the lateral retinaculum and quadriceps longitudinally, leaving an 8-10 mm lateral cuff at the patella; carry the split toward the lateral patellar-tendon border and dislocate the patella medially with knee flexion.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, lateral retinaculum, quadriceps tendon, capsule and synovium, then distal femoral articular surface.

structures_encountered.text: Quadriceps tendon, lateral patellar retinaculum, patella, patellar tendon, synovium, femoral condyles, trochlea, menisci, and cruciate region are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Patellar tendon insertion, articular cartilage, menisci, lateral superior genicular artery, and extensor-mechanism blood supply are at risk.

danger_zones.text: An incision or quadriceps split that is too short concentrates force at the patellar tendon during medial dislocation and can cause avulsion; lengthen the exposure rather than applying force.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the extensor mechanism gradually with the knee flexed; avoid focal pressure on patellar cartilage and excessive tension at the tibial tubercle.

exposure.text: Provides broad visualization of the distal femoral articular surface and lateral condyle while supporting lateral submuscular plate insertion.

limitations.text: Posterior condylar fragments may still need a fragment-specific exposure, and the approach disrupts the extensor mechanism more than a limited lateral plate approach.

extensions.text: Extend proximally through the quadriceps split, add a separate proximal lateral window for plate control, or use small aligned stab incisions for percutaneous screws.

indications.text: Use for intra-articular distal femoral fractures requiring direct reconstruction of the articular block and lateral fixation, including selected lateral sagittal or coronal patterns.

relative_contraindications.text: Prefer a more limited lateral exposure when no articular visualization is needed, and use a fragment-specific medial or posterior approach when the target cannot be seen safely from the lateral parapatellar corridor.

implant_implications.text: The approach accommodates lateral locked plating through a submuscular tunnel; confirm the proximal plate is centered before placing remaining proximal screws.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Obtain unobstructed AP, lateral, and oblique views to verify articular reduction, alignment, plate centering, screw length, and absence of joint penetration.

closure.text: Repair quadriceps tendon and the retained lateral parapatellar cuff with interrupted heavy sutures, restore retinacular continuity, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include patellar-tendon avulsion, extensor weakness or adhesions, stiffness, articular malreduction, infection, nonunion, malalignment, and hardware irritation.

bailouts.text: If the patella will not dislocate without excessive tension, extend the skin and quadriceps releases; add a fragment-specific approach if posterior or medial reduction remains unseen.

questions.question: Why must the incision and quadriceps split be long enough?
questions.answer: To permit medial patellar dislocation without avulsing the patellar tendon.

questions.question: How much retinacular cuff is retained beside the patella?
What vessel may be encountered laterally?
questions.answer: The lateral superior genicular artery, which may require avoidance or ligation.

approaches.name: Direct medial approach to the distal femur
approaches.region: medial distal thigh and distal femur
approaches.corridor: Posterior border of the adductor-magnus tendon with sartorius retracted posteriorly and vastus medialis anteriorly

sources.title: Medial Approach To The Distal Femur
Surgical approaches and outcomes associated with intra-articular Hoffa fractures
Current concepts in the treatment of distal femur fractures in adults

procedure_applications.condition: A medial condylar or medial Hoffa fragment needs direct medial reduction, limited posterior access, or associated popliteal vascular exploration

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee freely flexed; flexion relaxes medial tissues and permits posterior retraction of sartorius.

setup.text: Review CT for the medial and posterior fracture extent, prepare vascular instruments when arterial injury is suspected, and ensure access for orthogonal fluoroscopy.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the adductor tubercle, adductor-magnus tendon, medial epicondyle, medial joint line, patella, and expected course of the long saphenous vein.

incision.text: Make a straight longitudinal incision along the posterior border of the adductor-magnus tendon beginning near the adductor tubercle and extend proximally as required.

superficial_interval.text: Identify the anterior edge of sartorius and, with the knee flexed, retract sartorius posteriorly to expose the adductor-magnus tendon.

deep_interval.text: Retract adductor magnus and its tendon posteriorly and vastus medialis anteriorly to reach the medial femur; remain directly on bone when developing any posterior extension.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, sartorial fascia, sartorius-adductor region, interval between adductor magnus and vastus medialis, then medial femoral periosteum and optional capsule.

structures_encountered.text: Sartorius, adductor-magnus tendon, vastus medialis, medial distal femur, capsule, and posterior popliteal space may be encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Popliteal artery and vein, tibial nerve, saphenous nerve and vein, medial genicular vessels, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The popliteal neurovascular bundle lies immediately posterior to the distal femur; posterior dissection must be blunt, controlled, and performed with direct anatomic awareness.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid blind or forceful posterior retraction of adductor magnus and avoid prolonged compression of the popliteal bundle or traction on saphenous structures.

exposure.text: Exposes medial distal-femoral fractures and permits limited posterior access, possible popliteal vascular exploration, and extension toward the posterior cruciate ligament.

limitations.text: Posterior joint-surface visualization through a medial capsulotomy is limited; posterior coronal fragments may require a more specific exposure.

extensions.text: Extend proximally along adductor magnus, develop the posterior plane bluntly for vascular access, or add a capsulotomy for limited articular inspection.

indications.text: Use for medial distal-femoral or medial Hoffa fractures, selected posterior access, and distal-femur fractures complicated by suspected arterial injury.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose a parapatellar exposure when broad anterior articular reconstruction is required and a dedicated posterior or fragment-specific route when posterior visualization would otherwise be blind.

implant_implications.text: Supports medial buttress or fragment-specific fixation; drill and screw trajectories directed posteriorly require guarded depth because of the adjacent popliteal bundle.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, and condylar oblique views to verify medial reduction, posterior fragment position, implant containment, and screw length.

closure.text: Obtain meticulous hemostasis, repair any capsulotomy, allow the muscular interval to return anatomically, then close fascia, subcutaneous tissue, and skin in layers.

complications.text: Complications include popliteal neurovascular injury, saphenous neuropathy, hematoma, articular malreduction, stiffness, infection, nonunion, and symptomatic medial implants.

bailouts.text: If posterior control cannot be obtained safely, stop blind dissection and add a dedicated fragment-specific or posterior exposure with vascular assistance when indicated.

questions.question: What tendon guides the incision?
questions.answer: The adductor-magnus tendon at the adductor tubercle.

questions.question: What muscles are retracted to expose the femur?
questions.answer: Adductor magnus posteriorly and vastus medialis anteriorly.

questions.question: What is the major posterior danger?
questions.answer: The popliteal neurovascular bundle directly behind the distal femur.

approaches.name: Medial parapatellar approach to the distal femur
aliases: medial knee arthrotomy for distal femur
approaches.region: anterior medial knee and distal femur
approaches.corridor: Medial retinacular and capsular arthrotomy with lateral patellar dislocation and optional quadriceps extension

sources.title: Current concepts in the treatment of distal femur fractures in adults
Surgical approaches and outcomes associated with intra-articular Hoffa fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A medial condylar or intra-articular distal femur fracture needs broad anterior articular visualization
Retrograde nailing of an intra-articular distal extension requires medial parapatellar joint entry

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the knee freely flexed and the patella mobile enough for controlled lateral displacement.

setup.text: Prepare the entire limb, plan incision length from fracture morphology, and preserve options for proximal quadriceps extension and fluoroscopic retrograde-nail access.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the patella, patellar tendon, tibial tubercle, medial joint line, medial epicondyle, and course of the long saphenous vein.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal slightly oblique medial parapatellar incision from about 5 cm above the superior patellar pole toward the tibial tubercle without raising broad skin flaps.

superficial_interval.text: Preserve skin perfusion and the long saphenous vein where possible; expect small infrapatellar saphenous branches near the medial and inferior patella.

deep_interval.text: Incise the medial patellar retinaculum and capsule, lengthen proximally into quadriceps if needed, and dislocate the patella laterally with controlled knee flexion.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue with saphenous branches, medial retinaculum, joint capsule and synovium, then distal femoral articular surface.

structures_encountered.text: Medial retinaculum, capsule, patella, patellar tendon, quadriceps tendon, trochlea, femoral condyles, menisci, and cruciate region are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Infrapatellar saphenous branches, long saphenous vein, patellar tendon insertion, skin blood supply, menisci, and articular cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid broad skin flaps and forceful lateral patellar dislocation; inadequate release can avulse the patellar tendon from the tibial tubercle.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the extensor mechanism gently and distribute pressure away from patellar cartilage; lengthen the arthrotomy rather than levering against the tendon.

exposure.text: Provides wide anterior visualization of both femoral condyles and the articular surface for reconstruction and retrograde-nail entry.

limitations.text: Posterior Hoffa fragments may not be adequately visualized, and the approach does not provide the same direct medial extra-articular or vascular corridor as the adductor-magnus approach.

extensions.text: Extend proximally into quadriceps for broader distal-femur exposure or distally toward the tibial tubercle for additional joint access.

indications.text: Use for medial femoral-condylar and selected intra-articular distal-femur fractures, and as an access option for retrograde nailing.

relative_contraindications.text: Use a fragment-specific medial or posterior exposure when a posterior coronal fragment cannot be reduced safely through the anterior arthrotomy, and avoid compromised medial skin when another route is available.

implant_implications.text: Allows direct articular reduction and central retrograde-nail starting-point assessment; protect cartilage and verify that screws or nail components remain extra-articular.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use AP, lateral, notch, and condylar oblique views as appropriate to confirm articular congruity, retrograde entry, alignment, and implant containment.

closure.text: Repair capsule and medial retinaculum anatomically, close any quadriceps extension with heavy absorbable suture, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin without strangulating medial flaps.

complications.text: Complications include saphenous sensory disturbance or neuroma, patellar-tendon avulsion, wound compromise, extensor weakness, stiffness, infection, and articular malreduction.

bailouts.text: If lateral patellar displacement remains unsafe, extend the retinacular or quadriceps release; add a fragment-specific approach rather than accepting an unseen posterior reduction.

questions.question: Which sensory nerve branches are encountered medially?
questions.answer: Infrapatellar branches of the saphenous nerve.

questions.question: Why should broad skin flaps be avoided?
How is exposure increased proximally?
questions.answer: By extending the arthrotomy into the quadriceps tendon.
